blocks.body:
The series $\sum n^{-s}$ only converges for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. The functional equation is a symmetry relating the value of $\zeta$ at $s$ to its value at $1 - s$, so that once $\zeta$ is understood to the right of the critical strip it is understood to the left as well. Riemann proved it in 1859 using the theta function, and the proof is a model for every $L$-function that came after.

Its consequences are immediate and important: $\zeta$ continues to the whole plane, it vanishes at $-2, -4, -6, \dots$ (the trivial zeros), its remaining zeros are symmetric about the line $\operatorname{Re} s = \tfrac12$, its values at negative integers are rational, and its growth to the left of the strip can be read off from its growth to the right.

blocks.title: Riemann's idea: a Mellin transform of theta
blocks.body:
Start from the gamma integral of [[gamma]] with the substitution $x = \pi n^2t$: for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$,
$$\int_0^\infty e^{-\pi n^2t}\,t^{s/2}\,\frac{dt}{t} = \pi^{-s/2}\,n^{-s}\,\Gamma(s/2).$$
Sum over $n \ge 1$ when $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$; the double sum-integral of absolute values converges, so the swap is allowed:
$$\Lambda(s) := \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s) = \int_0^\infty\omega(t)\,t^{s/2}\,\frac{dt}{t}, \qquad \omega(t) = \sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi n^2t} = \frac{\theta(t) - 1}{2}.$$
In the language of [[mellin]], $\Lambda(s)$ is the Mellin transform of $\omega$ evaluated at $s/2$. As $t \to \infty$, $\omega(t)$ decays like $e^{-\pi t}$; as $t \to 0^+$ it blows up like $\tfrac12t^{-1/2}$, and that blow-up is why the integral converges only for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$. The theta law $\theta(1/t) = \sqrt t\,\theta(t)$ of [[fourier-poisson]] describes the blow-up exactly, and Riemann's idea is to use it to fold the bad half of the integral onto the good half.

blocks.title: Riemann's functional equation
blocks.body:
The function $\Lambda(s) = \pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$ extends to a meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ whose only poles are simple poles at $s = 0$ (residue $-1$) and $s = 1$ (residue $1$), and
$$\Lambda(s) = \Lambda(1-s).$$
Equivalently, the completed zeta function
$$\xi(s) = \tfrac12\,s(s-1)\,\pi^{-s/2}\,\Gamma(s/2)\,\zeta(s)$$
is entire and satisfies $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$. For all $s \ne 0, 1$,
$$\Lambda(s) = \frac{1}{s-1} - \frac1s + \int_1^\infty\omega(t)\bigl(t^{s/2} + t^{(1-s)/2}\bigr)\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ and split the integral for $\Lambda(s)$ at $t = 1$. In the piece over $(0,1)$ substitute $t = 1/u$:
$$\int_0^1\omega(t)\,t^{s/2}\,\frac{dt}{t} = \int_1^\infty\omega(1/u)\,u^{-s/2}\,\frac{du}{u}.$$
From $\theta(1/u) = \sqrt u\,\theta(u)$ we get $2\omega(1/u) + 1 = \sqrt u\,(2\omega(u) + 1)$, that is,
$$\omega(1/u) = \sqrt u\,\omega(u) + \tfrac12\sqrt u - \tfrac12.$$
Substituting,
$$\int_1^\infty\omega(1/u)\,u^{-s/2}\,\frac{du}{u} = \int_1^\infty\omega(u)\,u^{(1-s)/2}\,\frac{du}{u} + \frac12\int_1^\infty\bigl(u^{(1-s)/2} - u^{-s/2}\bigr)\frac{du}{u}.$$
For $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ the last integral is elementary: $\int_1^\infty u^{(1-s)/2-1}\,du = \frac{2}{s-1}$ and $\int_1^\infty u^{-s/2-1}\,du = \frac2s$, so the last term equals $\frac{1}{s-1} - \frac1s$. Adding the piece over $(1,\infty)$ gives the displayed formula for $\Lambda(s)$ when $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$.

Now examine the right side. For $t \ge 1$, $\omega(t) \le \sum_{n\ge1}e^{-\pi nt} \le e^{-\pi t}/(1 - e^{-\pi})$, so the integral converges absolutely and uniformly for $s$ in any compact set, and defines an entire function of $s$. The right side is therefore meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ with simple poles only at $s = 1$ (residue $1$) and $s = 0$ (residue $-1$), and it is the continuation of $\Lambda$. Replacing $s$ by $1 - s$ swaps $t^{s/2}$ and $t^{(1-s)/2}$ and turns $\frac{1}{s-1} - \frac1s$ into $\frac{1}{-s} - \frac{1}{1-s} = \frac{1}{s-1} - \frac1s$, so the right side is unchanged and $\Lambda(s) = \Lambda(1-s)$.

Finally, $\tfrac12s(s-1)$ vanishes simply at $0$ and $1$, cancelling both poles, so $\xi$ is entire; and $s(s-1)$ is invariant under $s \mapsto 1-s$, so $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$.

blocks.title: Continuation, trivial zeros and ζ(0)
blocks.body:
Since $1/\Gamma$ is entire, $\zeta(s) = \pi^{s/2}\Lambda(s)/\Gamma(s/2)$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$. Its possible poles are the poles of $\Lambda$, at $0$ and $1$. At $s = 0$ the pole of $\Lambda$ is cancelled by the zero of $1/\Gamma(s/2)$, so the only pole of $\zeta$ is at $s = 1$. This completes the proof of the continuation stated in [[zeta]].

Now use that $\Gamma(s/2)$ has simple poles at $s = 0, -2, -4, \dots$.
- At $s = -2k$ with $k \ge 1$: $$\Lambda(-2k) = \Lambda(1+2k) = \pi^{-(2k+1)/2}\Gamma(k+\tfrac12)\zeta(2k+1)$$ is finite and nonzero, while $1/\Gamma(s/2)$ has a simple zero. So $\zeta$ has a simple zero at each negative even integer. These are the trivial zeros.
- At $s = 0$: $\Lambda(s) = -\frac1s + O(1)$, while $\Gamma(s/2) = \frac2s + O(1)$, so $\pi^{s/2}/\Gamma(s/2) = \frac s2 + O(s^2)$. Multiplying, $\zeta(0) = -\tfrac12$.

blocks.title: Asymmetric form
blocks.body:
As meromorphic functions on $\mathbb C$,
$$\zeta(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi s}{2}\Bigr)\,\Gamma(1-s)\,\zeta(1-s).$$

From $\Lambda(s) = \Lambda(1-s)$,
$$\zeta(s) = \pi^{s-1/2}\,\frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{1-s}{2}\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac s2\bigr)}\,\zeta(1-s).$$
Two gamma identities simplify the ratio. The reflection formula of [[gamma]] gives $\frac{1}{\Gamma(s/2)} = \frac{\Gamma(1 - s/2)\sin(\pi s/2)}{\pi}$. Legendre's duplication formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(z + \tfrac12) = 2^{1-2z}\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(2z)$, which we quote (it follows from the Beta integral), with $z = \frac{1-s}{2}$ gives $\Gamma\bigl(\frac{1-s}{2}\bigr)\Gamma\bigl(1 - \frac s2\bigr) = 2^s\sqrt\pi\,\Gamma(1-s)$. Together,
$$\frac{\Gamma\bigl(\frac{1-s}{2}\bigr)}{\Gamma\bigl(\frac s2\bigr)} = 2^s\pi^{-1/2}\sin\Bigl(\frac{\pi s}{2}\Bigr)\Gamma(1-s),$$
and substituting gives the formula.

blocks.title: Zeros and symmetry
blocks.body:
Every nontrivial zero of $\zeta$ is a zero of $\xi$, and conversely. Indeed, for $\operatorname{Re} s > 1$ none of the factors of $\xi$ vanishes, so $\xi(s) \ne 0$ there; by the symmetry $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$, also $\xi(s) \ne 0$ for $\operatorname{Re} s < 0$. The trivial zeros of $\zeta$ are cancelled by the poles of $\Gamma(s/2)$, and $\xi(0) = \xi(1) = \tfrac12$. So the zeros of $\xi$ all lie in the closed strip $0 \le \operatorname{Re} s \le 1$, where they are exactly the zeros of $\zeta$. (They actually lie in the open strip, by the nonvanishing of $\zeta$ on $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$.)

Since $\xi$ is real on the real axis, $\xi(\bar s) = \overline{\xi(s)}$. Combined with $\xi(s) = \xi(1-s)$, zeros come in sets $\{\rho, \bar\rho, 1-\rho, 1-\bar\rho\}$, symmetric about the real axis and about the critical line $\operatorname{Re} s = \tfrac12$. On the critical line, $\xi(\tfrac12 + it) = \xi(\tfrac12 - it) = \overline{\xi(\tfrac12 + it)}$, so $t \mapsto \xi(\tfrac12+it)$ is a real function. Its sign changes locate zeros on the line; this is how zeros are computed, and it is the starting point of Hardy's 1914 proof that infinitely many zeros lie on the critical line.

The symmetry also transports information. Any region free of zeros next to the line $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$, for instance one of the form $\sigma > 1 - c/\log(|t|+2)$ from the theory of the [[zero-free-region]], is reflected into a region free of nontrivial zeros next to $\operatorname{Re} s = 0$.

blocks.title: Growth on vertical lines
blocks.body:
Write the asymmetric form as $\zeta(s) = \chi(s)\zeta(1-s)$ with $\chi(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\sin(\pi s/2)\Gamma(1-s)$. Stirling's formula shows that for fixed real $\sigma$,
$$|\chi(\sigma + it)| \sim \Bigl(\frac{|t|}{2\pi}\Bigr)^{1/2-\sigma} \qquad (|t| \to \infty).$$
To the right of the strip, say on $\operatorname{Re} s = 1 + \delta$, $\zeta$ is bounded above and below. So on $\operatorname{Re} s = -\delta$ the functional equation gives $|\zeta(-\delta + it)| \asymp |t|^{1/2+\delta}$. Interpolating between these two lines with the Phragmén–Lindelöf principle (a maximum principle for strips, which we do not prove) yields the convexity bound $\zeta(\tfrac12 + it) = O(|t|^{1/4+\varepsilon})$. The Lindelöf hypothesis asserts $O(|t|^\varepsilon)$; see [[lindelof]]. On the critical line itself $|\chi(\tfrac12 + it)| = 1$ exactly, so $|\zeta(\tfrac12 + it)| = |\zeta(\tfrac12 - it)|$.

blocks.title: Values at negative odd integers
blocks.body: Use the asymmetric form and Euler's formula for $\zeta(2k)$ to show that $\zeta(1 - 2k) = -\dfrac{B_{2k}}{2k}$ for $k \ge 1$. In particular $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$.
blocks.solution:
Put $s = 1 - 2k$, so $1 - s = 2k$. Then $\sin\bigl(\frac{\pi(1-2k)}{2}\bigr) = \cos(\pi k) = (-1)^k$ and $\Gamma(1-s) = \Gamma(2k) = (2k-1)!$, so
$$\zeta(1-2k) = 2^{1-2k}\pi^{-2k}(-1)^k(2k-1)!\,\zeta(2k).$$
Insert $\zeta(2k) = \frac{(-1)^{k+1}B_{2k}(2\pi)^{2k}}{2(2k)!}$ from [[zeta]]. The powers of $\pi$ cancel, $2^{1-2k}\cdot 2^{2k}/2 = 1$, the signs give $(-1)^{2k+1} = -1$, and $(2k-1)!/(2k)! = 1/(2k)$. Hence $\zeta(1-2k) = -B_{2k}/(2k)$.

For $k = 1$: $\zeta(-1) = -B_2/2 = -\tfrac{1}{12}$. Directly from the asymmetric form: $\zeta(-1) = 2^{-1}\pi^{-2}\sin(-\tfrac\pi2)\,\Gamma(2)\,\zeta(2) = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{1}{\pi^2}\cdot(-1)\cdot 1\cdot\tfrac{\pi^2}{6} = -\tfrac{1}{12}$.

blocks.title: A derivative at a trivial zero
blocks.solution:
Write $\zeta(s) = h(s)\sin(\pi s/2)$ with $h(s) = 2^s\pi^{s-1}\Gamma(1-s)\zeta(1-s)$, which is holomorphic near $s = -2$. Since $\sin(\pi s/2)$ vanishes at $s = -2$, the product rule gives
$$\zeta'(-2) = h(-2)\cdot\frac\pi2\cos(-\pi) = -\frac\pi2\,h(-2).$$
Now $h(-2) = 2^{-2}\pi^{-3}\Gamma(3)\zeta(3) = \frac{2\zeta(3)}{4\pi^3} = \frac{\zeta(3)}{2\pi^3}$, so $\zeta'(-2) = -\frac{\zeta(3)}{4\pi^2} \approx -0.03045$. In the same way (Exercise 4) every $\zeta'(-2k)$ is a rational multiple of $\zeta(2k+1)/\pi^{2k}$.

blocks.title: Where -1/12 really lives
blocks.body:
Show that as $y \to 0^+$,
$$\sum_{n\ge1}n\,e^{-ny} = \frac{1}{y^2} - \frac{1}{12} + O(y^2),$$
so that with $y = 1/N$ the smoothed sum of $1 + 2 + 3 + \cdots$ is $N^2 - \tfrac{1}{12} + O(N^{-2})$.
blocks.solution:
Mellin method. Since $\sum_n n\cdot n^{-s} = \zeta(s-1)$, the smoothed-sum formula of [[mellin]] gives, for $c > 2$,
$$\sum_{n\ge1}n\,e^{-ny} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\Gamma(s)\,\zeta(s-1)\,y^{-s}\,ds.$$
Shift the line to $\operatorname{Re} s = -\tfrac52$. This is allowed because $\zeta$ grows at most polynomially on vertical lines (the growth section above, with the convexity principle) while $\Gamma$ decays exponentially. The poles crossed are: $s = 2$, where $\zeta(s-1)$ has its pole, with residue $\Gamma(2)y^{-2} = y^{-2}$; $s = 0$, a pole of $\Gamma$ with residue $1$, contributing $\zeta(-1) = -\tfrac{1}{12}$; $s = -1$, contributing $-\zeta(-2)\,y = 0$; and $s = -2$, contributing $\tfrac12\zeta(-3)\,y^2 = \tfrac{y^2}{240}$. The integral on the new line is $O(y^{5/2})$. Hence the sum is $y^{-2} - \tfrac{1}{12} + \tfrac{y^2}{240} + O(y^{5/2})$.

Check by a closed form. Differentiating the geometric series, $\sum_n n e^{-ny} = \frac{e^{-y}}{(1-e^{-y})^2} = \frac{1}{4\sinh^2(y/2)}$, whose Laurent expansion is $\frac{1}{y^2} - \frac{1}{12} + \frac{y^2}{240} - \cdots$. The constant term $-\tfrac{1}{12}$ is $\zeta(-1)$, and it appears next to a main term $N^2$ that goes to infinity. That is the honest content of the slogan.

blocks.body:
- The functional equation does not say $|\zeta(s)| = |\zeta(1-s)|$. The factor $\chi(s)$ has size about $(|t|/2\pi)^{1/2-\sigma}$; only on the critical line are the two sizes equal.
- Symmetry about $\operatorname{Re} s = \tfrac12$ pairs zeros; it does not force them onto the line. That is the [[rh|Riemann hypothesis]], which remains open.
- The trivial zeros are zeros of $\zeta$ but not of $\xi$, since the poles of $\Gamma(s/2)$ absorb them. And $\zeta$ does not vanish at $0$ or at the negative odd integers.
- Normalisations differ. Riemann's own function was, in today's notation, $\xi(\tfrac12 + it)$ regarded as a function of $t$ (often written $\Xi(t)$), and some authors omit the factor $\tfrac12$ or work with $\Lambda$. Check before comparing formulas.

- [[nontrivial-zeros]]: $\xi$ is entire of order 1, which leads to Hadamard's product over the zeros; counting zeros up to height $T$ with the argument principle uses the functional equation to control the part of the contour left of the strip, giving the Riemann–von Mangoldt formula $N(T) = \frac{T}{2\pi}\log\frac{T}{2\pi} - \frac{T}{2\pi} + O(\log T)$.
- [[lindelof]]: the convexity bound $|t|^{1/4+\varepsilon}$ comes from the functional equation; any improvement is a subconvexity bound.
- [[hecke-l]] and [[dedekind-zeta]]: Hecke carried the same template (theta function, Poisson summation, Mellin transform, fold at $t = 1$) to Dedekind zeta functions and to the $L$-functions now named after him.
- [[l-functions]] and [[gauss-sums]]: for a primitive Dirichlet character the theta function is twisted by $\chi$, and the Gauss sum $\tau(\chi)$ enters the functional equation as the root number factor.
- [[zero-free-region]]: the symmetry turns a zero-free region near $\operatorname{Re} s = 1$ into one near $\operatorname{Re} s = 0$.

1. Show that $\xi(0) = \xi(1) = \tfrac12$.
2. Use the asymmetric form with $\zeta(4) = \pi^4/90$ and $\zeta(6) = \pi^6/945$ to show $\zeta(-3) = \tfrac{1}{120}$ and $\zeta(-5) = -\tfrac{1}{252}$.
3. Show that $\xi(s)$ is real when $s$ is real and when $s$ lies on the critical line.
4. Show that $\zeta'(-2k) = (-1)^k\dfrac{(2k)!\,\zeta(2k+1)}{2\,(2\pi)^{2k}}$ for every integer $k \ge 1$.

sources.ref: Titchmarsh, The Theory of the Riemann Zeta-Function
